comparability.reason: Matrix effects were evaluated by testing Milli-Q water, groundwater, and two laundry wastewaters under matched operating conditions (same PFAS spike concentrations, identical adsorbent doses, and 24-h contact time in the same batch configuration). This supports direct comparison of PFAS adsorption performance and allows attribution of differences primarily to matrix composition, especially organic matter in wastewater.

endpoints.interpretation: Adsorption isotherms for PFOA, PFOS, and GenX on AC and BC-W were obtained in Milli-Q water, groundwater, and two wastewaters after 24 h, and fitted predominantly to Freundlich models (Langmuir for GenX on BC-W). These isotherms quantify sorbed mass per mass of adsorbent as a function of equilibrium concentration for each matrix.

endpoints.interpretation: PFAS removal efficiencies were compared across matrices under matched conditions (identical PFAS spikes, adsorbent dose, and contact time). PFAS removal in groundwater remained effective and was similar to or higher than that in Milli-Q water, whereas removal declined in wastewater, especially for PFOA, due to competition from organic matter.

endpoints.interpretation: Across all tested matrices, AC and BC-W exhibited substantial adsorption capacities of approximately 7.7 mg/g (PFOA), 16.1 mg/g (PFOS), and 4.8 mg/g (GenX), indicating robust PFAS uptake even when matrix constituents such as natural organic matter are present, though with reduced performance in wastewater compared to Milli-Q and groundwater.
endpoints.reported_term: adsorption capacities across matrices

endpoints.interpretation: In wastewater matrices, dissolved organic matter competitively occupied adsorption sites, leading to reduced PFAS adsorption, particularly for PFOA, relative to Milli-Q water and groundwater. In contrast, groundwater constituents did not significantly diminish PFAS removal under the tested high-concentration conditions.
endpoints.reported_term: matrix effect mechanism – organic matter competition

limitations.statement: Adsorption isotherms in the different matrices were generated with a limited number of data points, which could reduce the robustness of model fitting.

endpoints.interpretation: Lower qe in multispecies systems implies reduced removal capacity per unit GAC in the presence of multiple co-occurring PFAS compared with single-compound tests under otherwise matched conditions.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS removal via adsorption

limitations.statement: Isotherms do not directly evaluate adsorption breakthrough, so modeling tools (e.g., AdDesignS) are required to relate isotherm parameters to full- or pilot-scale GAC system performance. Parameters obtained with ground GAC may need adjustment for particle size effects.
The study did not investigate competition with non-PFAS adsorbable synthetic organic compounds, so matrix effects from other organic contaminants were not characterized.
Bench-scale batch isotherms in standardized Type 1 water may not capture hydraulic, kinetic, and heterogeneity factors present in full-scale GAC contactors.

comparability.reason: NOM-free, NOM co-loaded, and NOM-preloaded conditions were tested using the same standardized water, GAC, and batch isotherm protocol, with differences arising from NOM and CaSO4 amendments; this design allows direct comparison of NOM-related matrix effects on qe across PFAS.

endpoints.interpretation: Percent qe difference relative to a mineral salt buffered isotherm baseline was used to quantify how NOM (with/without CaSO4, co-loading vs preloading) altered PFAS adsorption capacities for individual PFAS.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS adsorption capacity (qe) and percent qe difference relative to mineral salt buffered isotherm (MSBI)

endpoints.interpretation: More negative percent qe differences in NOM-amended systems indicate reduced PFAS removal capacity on GAC compared with NOM-free baseline conditions.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS removal via adsorption in presence of NOM

endpoints.interpretation: Shifts toward more negative percent qe difference when NOM was preloaded (vs co-loaded) suggest that pore blockage, in addition to direct competition, hindered PFAS adsorption; variability among PFAS (e.g., stronger negative impacts on PFHxS, PFOS, PFNA) points to PFAS- and NOM-property-dependent mechanisms.
endpoints.reported_term: NOM impact mechanism (competition vs pore blockage)

limitations.statement: The NOM impact evaluation focused on a specific NOM source and did not explore how different NOM types or compositions might alter PFAS adsorption or competitive mechanisms.

The study examined NOM and major ions, but it did not investigate competition with non-PFAS adsorbable synthetic organic compounds, limiting the applicability of findings to matrices containing other adsorbable organics.
